core: working definition: epidemiology is the study of the distribution and determinants of health-related states or events in specified populations, and the application of this study to the control of health problems (CDC Principles of Epidemiology)
the questions it asks: the five W's — what (health event), who (person), where (place), when (time), why (causes/risk factors)
distribution as frequency plus pattern across time, place, and person
tools: counting cases, comparing groups, tracking illness over time
the epidemiologic triad: agent, host, and environment as the framework for determinants
descriptive epidemiology (who, where, when) versus analytic epidemiology (testing why, by comparing groups)
epidemiology in action: outbreak investigations and prevention planning
honest framing: epidemiology finds patterns and associations, not certainties
supporting: the contrast 'the clinician's patient is the individual; the epidemiologist's patient is the community'
CDC EIS Field Epidemiology Manual outbreak-investigation sequence (confirm and verify, define cases, count, describe by person/place/time, generate and test hypotheses, control measures, communicate)
the role of case definitions and comparison groups in giving counts meaning

claims.claim: Epidemiology is defined by the CDC's Principles of Epidemiology as the study of the distribution and determinants of health-related states or events in specified populations, and the application of this study to the control of health problems.

Epidemiologic investigation is organized by five questions — what (the health event and case definition), who (person), where (place), when (time), and why (causes and risk factors) — and distribution is described by frequency and by pattern across time, place, and person.

Epidemiology studies populations rather than individuals: the clinician's patient is the individual while the epidemiologist's patient is the community, so epidemiologists count cases and interpret them against valid comparison groups.

Disease occurrence is organized by the epidemiologic triad of agent, host, and environment; the elements interact, so a disease agent causes illness only where susceptible hosts and permitting environmental conditions meet, and prevention can target any of the three.

Descriptive epidemiology characterizes the distribution of disease by person, place, and time (who, where, when), while analytic epidemiology tests hypotheses about causes and risk factors, typically by comparing groups such as the exposed and the unexposed.

Epidemiologic findings are patterns and associations, not proofs of causation: hypotheses generated from descriptive patterns must be tested, and conclusions are drawn with judgment about the strength of the evidence.

Epidemiology in action includes outbreak investigation following the CDC EIS field manual sequence — confirm the outbreak and verify the diagnosis, define what counts as a case, find and count cases, describe them by person, place, and time, generate and test hypotheses about the source, implement control measures, and communicate findings.

conflictingEvidence.issue: Association versus causation in epidemiologic findings
positions: Descriptive and observational patterns reveal associations (e.g., the sick group more often ate a suspect food) but cannot by themselves prove causation
Causal conclusions require analytic comparison, testing, and judgment; outbreak responses often act on strong patterns before proof is complete
conflictingEvidence.resolution: Lesson presents findings as patterns, not certainties, and shows investigation moving from description to hypothesis testing to action — faithful to both the textbook's caution and the field manual's action-oriented sequence.

conflictingEvidence.issue: How the five W's are framed
positions: The CDC textbook presents five W's: what (health event), who, where, when, and why
Popular summaries sometimes compress the list to who, where, when, and why, treating the health event (what) as already known
conflictingEvidence.resolution: Lesson presents the full five W's with 'what' as the health event and case definition, and notes that who/where/when describe distribution while why reaches for determinants.

positions: The epidemiologic triad (agent, host, environment) frames disease as the interaction of three elements
Real diseases often involve many co-factors beyond three simple categories, and the triad is a deliberate simplification
conflictingEvidence.resolution: Lesson presents the triad as an organizing framework for thinking about determinants, explicitly noting that disease usually arises from interaction among the elements rather than a single cause.
